terminal.description: A shell in your workspace. Build the states here and run them, after you call your functions from main.

tasks.title: Name the states of a repair
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 1` in `src/status.cpp`, write an `enum class` called `Status` with four values: `Waiting`, `OnBench`, `Ready` and `Collected`.

Check asks the compiler whether `Status` is an `enum class`, reads each of the four values, and makes sure no two of them are the same.
nextSteps: Inside, write the four values, separated by commas.
In `main`, make a `Status` variable with one of the values.
hints: An `enum class` is a type whose values are names you choose. It ends with a semicolon after its `}`, like a struct.
Give the values no numbers: the compiler numbers them one after another by itself, so each is a value of its own.
The shape is `enum class Status { Waiting, OnBench, Ready, Collected };`.

tasks.title: Say whether a repair can be collected
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 2`, write a function called `canCollect` that takes a state as a `Status` and gives back `true` when it is `Ready`, and `false` for every other state.

Check calls `canCollect` with each of the four states and reads what it gives back. It uses a `Status` of its own here, written as Task 1 asks, so this task is judged on its own.
nextSteps: Write the first line: a `Status` in, a `bool` back.
Compare the state with one value of `Status`, written with its type's name.
Give back the result of that comparison.
hints: A value of an enum class is always written with its type's name in front, like `Status::Waiting`. Alone, the compiler does not know the name.
Compare with `==`, as with numbers. A value of an enum class is never compared with a number.

tasks.title: Write a state in words for the slip
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 3`, write a function called `statusText` that takes a state as a `Status` and gives back its words as a `std::string`, chosen with a `switch` that has a case for each of the four states and no `default`:

| State | Words |
| --- | --- |
| `Waiting` | `waiting for the bench` |
| `OnBench` | `on the bench` |
| `Ready` | `ready to collect` |
| `Collected` | `collected` |

Check looks for the `switch` and for no `default` in `statusText`, then calls it with each state and reads what it gives back. A state without a case is a warning from the compiler, and Check counts it as a mistake.
nextSteps: Write the first line: a `Status` in, a `std::string` back.
Give each of the four states its own `case`, ending in a `return` of its words.
After the `switch`, write one more `return`, as the lesson explains.
hints: `switch (status)` jumps to the `case` whose value is the state. Each case is written `case Status::Waiting:`.
A case that ends without `return` or `break` runs on into the case below it. Leave out `default`, so the compiler warns when a state has no case.
The shape is `switch (status) { case Status::Waiting: return "waiting for the bench"; ... } return "";`, with a case for each state.

tasks.title: Move a repair on to its next state
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 4`, write a function called `nextStatus` that takes a state as a `Status` and gives back the state that comes after it: `OnBench` after `Waiting`, `Ready` after `OnBench`, `Collected` after `Ready`. `Collected` is the last state, so after `Collected` it is still `Collected`.

Check calls `nextStatus` with each of the four states and reads the state it gives back.
nextSteps: Write the first line: a `Status` in, a `Status` back.
Decide what comes after each state, with a `switch` or with `if`.
Give back a value of `Status` each time, never a number.
In `main`, move a repair on twice and print its words.
hints: A function can give back a value of an enum class, written with its type's name, like `return Status::OnBench;`.
Two cases can share one `return`: write `case Status::Ready:` and `case Status::Collected:` one under the other.
The shape is a `switch` like Task 3's, where each case gives back a state instead of words.
